If you can rest in that, you can afford to be charitable about the thousand years. The kingdom does not depend on us getting the chart right. It depends on the King, and He is not in doubt.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The three historic positions are premillennialism (Christ returns before a literal earthly thousand-year reign), amillennialism (the millennium is the present reign of Christ between His comings, with His return bringing the final judgment and new creation), and postmillennialism (Christ returns after a gospel-driven golden age). Premillennialism appears in early fathers like Irenaeus and Justin Martyr and dominates much modern evangelicalism, especially in its dispensational form. Amillennialism, shaped by Augustine, has been the majority view in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and much Reformed thought. Postmillennialism flourished among Puritans and nineteenth-century Protestants. None is excluded by the ecumenical creeds, and all affirm Christ's reign, His return, final judgment, and the new creation.

questions.question: Who or what is the antichrist?
questions.category: Last things and the return of Christ
questions.shortAnswer: The antichrist is the great opponent of Christ at the end of the age, described as a deceiver who exalts himself against God. Scripture also says many antichrists are already at work, so the term names both a coming figure and a spirit of opposition present in every era.
questions.answer:
The word antichrist appears far less in the Bible than the cultural noise around it would suggest, and only in the letters of John. There he writes that his readers have heard the antichrist is coming, and that even now many antichrists have come, which is how they know it is the last hour (1 John 2:18). For John, an antichrist is anyone who denies that Jesus is the Christ, who denies the Father and the Son, who refuses to confess Jesus come in the flesh (1 John 2:22, 4:3). So the first thing Scripture does with the term is widen it. The antichrist is not only a single future villain. It is a spirit of denial already loose in the world, and it works through false teaching, not just political power.

Alongside this, the New Testament does point to a climactic figure. Paul warns the Thessalonians of the man of lawlessness, the son of destruction, who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god, taking his seat in the temple of God and proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). Paul says this figure is currently restrained and will be revealed at the proper time, and that the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of His mouth at His coming. This is a real and disturbing prophecy of a final, concentrated rebellion, an idolatry of self that reaches its peak just before Christ returns to end it.

The book of Revelation adds the imagery most people associate with the antichrist, though it never uses the word. There are two beasts, one from the sea and one from the earth, and the famous number 666, the number of the beast and of a man (Revelation 13:18). In its first-century setting, this language pointed unmistakably at the Roman Empire and its cult of emperor worship, which demanded that Caesar be honored as lord and god. The beast is tyranny that claims the worship owed to God alone. Many scholars note that the number 666, by the ancient practice of assigning numbers to letters, fits the name Nero Caesar, the emperor who persecuted Christians. So Revelation's beast had a concrete, present referent even as it pictures a recurring and final pattern.

This is why I think the wisest approach holds three things together. There is a spirit of antichrist, present in every age, wherever Christ is denied and human power claims divine honors. There have been many antichrist figures across history, tyrants and false teachers who embody that spirit, and the church has variously and often recklessly identified them, including Reformers who called the papacy antichrist and others who pinned the label on Nero, Hitler, Stalin, and a long line of contemporary figures who all turned out not to end the world. And there appears to be a final antichrist, a last and fullest embodiment of the rebellion, revealed just before the end. These are not competing readings so much as layers of the same reality.

What strikes me most, pastorally, is what John does with the doctrine. He does not use it to fuel speculation or fear. He uses it to test confession and to steady believers. The mark of antichrist is not a barcode or a political party. It is the denial of Jesus as the Christ come in the flesh. That means the most important antichrist detector is not watching the news but examining what a teacher says about Jesus. The deception John warns about is doctrinal before it is political, and it often comes from inside the religious community, dressed in the language of faith.

So resist two errors. Do not obsess, building elaborate identifications of the antichrist with whichever leader you fear, a game the church has played and lost for two thousand years. And do not dismiss, pretending there is no real and personal evil arrayed against Christ. The sober truth is in between. The spirit of antichrist is real and present, a final reckoning is coming, and Christ has already guaranteed the outcome. Paul does not tell the Thessalonians to be afraid of the man of lawlessness. He tells them how the story ends, with the Lord overthrowing him by the brightness of His coming. The antichrist, whoever and whenever, loses.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on whether the antichrist is primarily a single future individual, a succession of figures, a system or institution, or chiefly a spirit of opposition. Dispensational premillennialists typically expect a specific end-times world ruler who makes a covenant and is revealed during the tribulation. Many Reformers, including Luther and the Westminster Confession in its original form, identified the papacy as antichrist, a view few hold today. Preterists tie the beast and the man of lawlessness largely to Nero and first-century Rome. Amillennialists often see the antichrist as a recurring pattern of opposition culminating in a final figure. Catholic and Orthodox traditions generally expect a personal antichrist near the end while reading John's many antichrists as present heresy. All agree Christ defeats him decisively.

questions.question: Is the world really going to end? And should that scare me?
questions.category: Last things and the return of Christ
questions.shortAnswer: The present order of things will come to a decisive end when Christ returns, but the Bible's hope is not annihilation. It is renewal, the world remade rather than erased. For those in Christ, the end is not something to dread but something to long for.
questions.answer:
Yes, the Bible teaches that the world as we know it is heading toward an end. This is not a fearful add-on but part of the basic Christian view of history. Time is not an endless circle, the same seasons turning forever. It is a line with a beginning, when God created, and a destination, when God will bring all things to their appointed conclusion. Peter writes that the day of the Lord will come, and that the heavens will pass away and the elements will be dissolved (2 Peter 3:10). Jesus said heaven and earth will pass away, though His words will not (Matthew 24:35). So the honest answer is that this present order is not permanent.

But we have to be careful what we mean by end, because the popular imagination jumps straight to destruction, a planet incinerated, everything lost. The Bible's picture is stranger and far better. The same Peter who speaks of the heavens passing away goes on to say that we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Paul says creation itself waits with eager longing to be set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:21). The word often used is not destruction but renewal. What ends is the world's bondage to sin, death, and corruption. What remains, transfigured, is the world itself.

The best analogy is the resurrection of Jesus, which is the template for everything God intends to do with creation. His body in the tomb was not annihilated and replaced with a brand new one. It was the same body, raised, transformed, glorified, recognizable yet changed, no longer subject to death. So it will be with the cosmos. The end of the world is less like a building being demolished and more like a body being raised. There is real death involved, a genuine passing away, and then there is real continuity on the far side of it. The world dies and rises.

Should this scare you. The Bible's answer depends entirely on whose you are. For those who have built their whole existence on the present order, who have no hope beyond it and no peace with the God who made it, the end is rightly sobering. The same passages that promise renewal also promise judgment, a real accounting before a holy God (Revelation 20:11-15). I will not soften that, because softening it would be a kind of lying. But for those who belong to Christ, the tone of the New Testament is not terror. It is longing. The early Christians prayed for the end to come, because the end is when their Lord appears and their tears are wiped away.

This reframes how a Christian holds anxiety about the world. We are surrounded by end-of-the-world fears, ecological, nuclear, technological, and these fears are not foolish. Real catastrophes are possible, and we should work against them, because loving our neighbor includes the world our neighbor lives in. But the Christian is not finally at the mercy of these fears, because our hope was never that humanity would manage to keep the planet running forever by its own competence. Our hope is that the God who made it will redeem it. That frees us to work hard and to rest deep at the same time.

So I would say this to a frightened heart. Yes, this world will end, but ending is not the worst thing, and for the people of God it is not even a sad thing. The last word in the Bible is not a mushroom cloud. It is a city coming down out of heaven, a wedding, a God who dwells with His people and wipes every tear from their eyes, and a voice from the throne saying He is making all things new (Revelation 21:1-5). The end you are afraid of is not the end the Bible promises. The real end is a beginning that does not stop.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians agree the present order ends at Christ's return but differ on the nature of that end. Some emphasize a more literal destruction of the present cosmos followed by a fresh creation, reading 2 Peter 3 as the elements being burned up. Others, increasingly common in recent theology, emphasize continuity and renewal, reading the same passages as purifying judgment that transforms rather than annihilates, with the resurrection of Jesus as the model. There are also differences over timing tied to the millennial views, and over how literally to read apocalyptic imagery. Across these views, Christians share the conviction that history is heading toward Christ's return, a real judgment, and the new creation, not toward meaningless oblivion.

questions.question: What is the new heaven and new earth? Is heaven really our final home?
questions.category: Last things and the return of Christ
questions.shortAnswer: The new heaven and new earth is the renewed creation where God dwells with His people forever, the true and final home of the redeemed. Our ultimate hope is not to escape to heaven but for heaven and earth to be joined and made new.
questions.answer:
Most Christians, if asked where they will end up, would say heaven, picturing a place far off and elsewhere, immaterial, where saved souls float free of bodies and the earth is left behind. It is worth saying clearly that this is not quite the Bible's final picture. The New Testament's ultimate hope is not a one-way trip away from creation. It is the renewal of creation and the descent of God's presence into it. John writes that he saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, and a loud voice said that the dwelling place of God is now with man (Revelation 21:2-3). Notice the direction. The city comes down. God comes to dwell with us, here, in a remade world.

This fulfills a thread that runs from the very beginning. The Bible opens with God walking with humanity in a garden, heaven and earth overlapping, no separation between God's space and ours. Sin tore that apart and drove humanity out. The whole story since is God working to bring His presence back to His people. The tabernacle and temple were partial, localized returns of that presence. The incarnation, God dwelling among us in Christ, was the decisive one. And the new creation is the consummation, the moment heaven and earth are finally and fully reunited, and the prayer Jesus taught us, that God's will be done on earth as it is in heaven, is answered completely.

The scholar N. T. Wright has spent much of his career recovering this point for a church that had drifted into a vague heaven-as-escape spirituality, and he argues persuasively that the biblical hope is resurrection life in a renewed physical creation, not disembodied existence in a cloudy elsewhere. This matters enormously. It means the resurrection of the body is not a strange appendix to the faith but its very heart. We will not be ghosts. We will be raised, embodied, like the risen Christ, to live embodied lives in a real and renewed world. Isaiah pictured it as building houses and planting vineyards and enjoying the work of our hands, no longer in vain (Isaiah 65:21-23).

What will it be like. Scripture is restrained, and we should be too, but it gives us the shape. There will be no more death, no mourning, no crying, no pain, for the former things will have passed away (Revelation 21:4). There will be no temple in the city, because God Himself and the Lamb are its temple, the very thing every temple ever pointed toward (Revelation 21:22). There will be no sun, because the glory of God will be its light. And there will be the nations and their kings bringing their glory into it, which many take to mean that the redeemed cultures and achievements of human history, purified, are carried into the new world rather than discarded. Nothing good is finally wasted.

What does this do to how we live now. C. S. Lewis argued that the Christians who did most for the present world were precisely those who thought most of the next, and that aiming at heaven, you get earth thrown in, while aiming at earth you get neither. A solid hope in the new creation is not escapism. It is the opposite. If matter matters, if bodies will be raised and the earth renewed, then what we do with our bodies and our world now is not throwaway. Our labor in the Lord is not in vain, because it is somehow taken up into the world that lasts. The new creation dignifies the present one even as it relativizes it.

So is heaven our final home. In a sense, yes, but only because heaven is coming here. The believer who dies goes to be with Christ, which Paul calls far better, and that intermediate state is real comfort. But it is not the end of the story. The end of the story is resurrection and a renewed creation, God dwelling with His people in a world made whole, every tear wiped away by His own hand. We do not finally go up to God. He comes down to us, and stays. That is the home we were made for, and it is the home that is coming.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: There is broad agreement across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions on the core hope of resurrection and the new creation, all confessed in the creeds. Differences arise over emphasis and detail. Some traditions and popular piety stress the intermediate state and a more spiritual heaven, while recent biblical scholarship (notably N. T. Wright) has pressed the church to recover the bodily resurrection and renewed earth as the final hope. Catholics and Orthodox include purgation or purification of the soul before final glory, which most Protestants reject. There are differences over how literally to read Revelation's imagery and over the degree of continuity between this creation and the next. The shared conviction is that God will dwell forever with a redeemed, resurrected people in a renewed creation.

questions.question: What is the final judgment, and how should I think about being judged by God?
questions.category: Last things and the return of Christ
questions.shortAnswer: The final judgment is the day when the risen Christ judges every person who has ever lived, exposing all things and setting everything right. For those in Christ it is not a threat but a vindication, because the verdict has already been settled at the cross.
questions.answer:
Every culture has some instinct that wrongs must be answered, that the murderer who dies comfortably in old age has not actually gotten away with it, that the abused child crying in the dark deserves more than a shrug from the universe. The doctrine of final judgment takes that instinct and says it is true. History will not simply trail off into forgetfulness. There is a day appointed when God will judge the world in righteousness through the man He has appointed, and He has given assurance of this by raising Him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The Judge is Jesus, and His own resurrection is the down payment that the day is coming.

We have to feel the weight of it before we feel the comfort. Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10). John sees the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books are opened, and each is judged according to what he has done (Revelation 20:12). This is not a vague accounting. It is a real exposure of real lives, including the parts we have hidden from everyone, including ourselves. Jesus said that on the day of judgment people will give account even for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). Nothing is overlooked. That should sober anyone, and it sobers me when I let it.

But here is where the gospel changes the entire character of the day for the believer. The astonishing claim of the New Testament is that the verdict has already been announced in advance. The judgment that belongs to the last day has been brought forward to the cross, where Christ bore the condemnation His people deserved, so that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The Judge is the one who was judged in our place. This means the Christian does not approach the judgment seat hoping the scales tip in their favor. They approach it clothed in a righteousness that is not their own, with the verdict already spoken over them in the resurrection of their Substitute.

This is why the New Testament can speak of believers facing the judgment with confidence rather than terror. John writes that love has been perfected among us so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as He is, so also are we in this world, and perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:17-18). Read that slowly. The Christian's confidence on the last day is not arrogance and not denial of sin. It is the settled assurance that the One who will judge is the One who already loved us to death and back. You do not need to fear the verdict of a Judge who has already given His life to secure your acquittal.

At the same time, Scripture speaks of a real assessment of the believer's life and works, not to determine salvation but to reveal and reward what was built on the foundation of Christ. Paul says each one's work will be tested by fire, and if it survives, he will receive a reward, but if it is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, only as through fire (1 Corinthians 3:13-15). So the judgment is not a flat formality even for the saved. Our lives matter, our faithfulness matters, what we did with what we were given matters. Grace does not make our choices weightless. It makes them safe enough to be honest about.

So how should you think about being judged. If you are not yet Christ's, the judgment is the most serious news in the world, and the right response is not to manage your fear but to flee to the only one who can stand in your place. If you are His, the final judgment is, strangely, good news, the day evil is finally named and ended, the day every hidden faithfulness is brought to light, the day the Judge who died for you welcomes you home. The same event is terror to the unforgiven and homecoming to the forgiven. The difference is not how good you managed to be. The difference is whose you are when the books are opened.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians broadly affirm a final judgment by Christ, confessed in the creeds, but differ on its details. Catholics hold a particular judgment at death followed by the general judgment, and include purgatory as a purification for the saved before final glory, which Protestants reject. Reformed and Lutheran traditions stress justification by faith alone, so the believer's judgment confirms rather than determines a salvation already secured, with a separate assessment of works for reward. Eastern Orthodoxy emphasizes theosis and is often less juridical in its framing. Christians also disagree over the final state of the unjudged or unevangelized, and over whether the lost suffer eternal conscious punishment, conditional immortality (annihilation), or, as a minority hold, eventual restoration. All affirm Christ as the appointed Judge.
